easy.prompt: A team splits housing data into train, validation, and test sets. What is each split for?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Train a predictor; validation tunes settings; test estimates final performance once.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Train fits weights; validation adds more training data; test speeds up training.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Train selects features; validation labels the data; test trains the final model.

choices.label: D
choices.body: All three splits are used together to fit weights for maximum accuracy.

easy.hint: Next step: ask which split is allowed to change your choice of settings.
easy.explanation: Each split has one job: fit, select, then estimate once on unseen data.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: training minimizes loss to set weights. Step 2: validation compares settings like depth or learning rate. Step 3: the test set is locked away until the end for one unbiased estimate. Step 4: mixing roles leaks information and biases the estimate.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Validation never trains weights; it only compares already-trained models.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Labels come with the data; validation does not label anything.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Fitting on all splits destroys the unbiased estimate of new-data error.

easy.prompt: Which learning-curve pattern signals overfitting on a spam classifier?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Training loss keeps falling but validation loss rises.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Both training and validation loss fall together.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Training accuracy is low and validation accuracy is equally low.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Test accuracy is higher than training accuracy.

easy.hint: Next step: compare the direction of the two curves, not their absolute values.
easy.explanation: Overfitting is memorization: train improves while held-out validation worsens.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: falling train loss means the model keeps memorizing. Step 2: rising validation loss means new-data error grows. Step 3: the gap between them is the overfitting signal. Step 4: matched falling losses instead mean healthy learning.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Both falling means the model still generalizes; keep training.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Both bad means underfitting, a model too simple or undertrained.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Test above train is rare luck or leakage, not the overfitting signature.

easy.prompt: What is the correct order for using train, validation, and test splits?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Fit on train, pick settings on validation, report once on test.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Fit on test, pick settings on train, report on validation.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Fit on all data, then split and report the best split score.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Fit three models, one per split, and average their test scores.

easy.hint: Next step: check which split your decision depends on.
easy.explanation: The safe order is fit on train, select on validation, evaluate once on test.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: fit weights only on train. Step 2: use validation scores to choose depth or regularization. Step 3: freeze everything, then evaluate once on test. Step 4: any reuse of test for choices makes the final number optimistic.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Fitting on test leaks the answers; test must stay untouched until the end.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Reporting the best split after seeing all data is selection bias.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Averaging models trained on test still leaks test information.

easy.prompt: You try 5 tree depths for a loan model. How do you use the splits correctly?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Try 5 depths, pick the best validation score, and evaluate that one model once on test.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Try 5 depths, pick the best test score as the final result.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Try 5 depths on test, then re-split test to confirm.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Skip validation and tune depths directly on the full dataset.

easy.hint: Next step: ask which split each of your 5 comparisons touches.
easy.explanation: Tune on validation; the test set is used exactly once for the final estimate.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: train 5 models on train only. Step 2: rank them by validation error, which neither trained them nor is the final report. Step 3: take only the winner to test, once. Step 4: with 5 tries on test instead, the best of 5 is optimistic by selection bias.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Picking the best test score uses test for tuning, biasing it upward.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Re-splitting test after tuning does not undo the leak.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Tuning on all data leaves no unbiased estimate of new-data error.

easy.prompt: While tuning regularization strength, which score should guide your choice?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Validation score

choices.label: B
choices.body: Training score

choices.label: C
choices.body: Test score during tuning

choices.label: D
choices.body: Score on duplicated training rows

easy.hint: Next step: eliminate the split that is optimistic and the one that is locked.
easy.explanation: The validation score is the honest guide for settings; train is optimistic and test is locked.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: training score is biased because the model memorized it. Step 2: test is off-limits during tuning. Step 3: validation is held out from fitting but available for comparison. Step 4: duplicates of train rows measure memorization, not generalization.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Training error is optimistically biased; stronger fit always lowers it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Peeking at test during tuning leaks it into your decisions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Duplicates of train rows reward memorization, not new-data skill.

easy.prompt: Which practice is test-set tuning (a form of leakage)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Checking test accuracy after every tuning tweak to steer the next tweak.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Checking validation accuracy after every tuning tweak.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Retraining the final model on train plus validation before one test report.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Plotting training loss to confirm optimization works.

easy.hint: Next step: count how many decisions the test set influenced.
easy.explanation: Repeatedly steering by test turns test into a second validation set and biases it.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: each peek at test informs your next choice. Step 2: after 20 peeks you selected the luckiest of 20 on that sample. Step 3: the reported number is then biased upward. Step 4: validation peeks are fine because validation is designated for selection.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Using validation for decisions is its exact purpose.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Retraining on train+val after freezing choices is standard and safe.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Monitoring train loss checks optimization, not generalization.

easy.prompt: For predicting house prices ($), which loss function fits the task?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Squared error, because price is continuous.

choices.label: B
choices.body: 0-1 error, because price is continuous.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Hinge loss, because price is continuous.

choices.label: D
choices.body: BLEU score, because price is continuous.

easy.hint: Next step: ask whether the target is a number or a category.
easy.explanation: Regression with continuous targets calls for squared (or absolute) error.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: house price is a real number, a regression target. Step 2: squared error penalizes the residual y minus prediction. Step 3: 0-1 and hinge need discrete classes. Step 4: BLEU measures text overlap, irrelevant here.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 0-1 error counts misclassifications; it needs discrete labels.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Hinge loss is for margin classifiers, not continuous targets.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: BLEU scores generated text, not numeric predictions.

easy.prompt: For MNIST digit classification, which loss fits the task?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Cross-entropy on predicted probabilities, because the target is a class.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Squared error on class indices 0/1/2 treated as numbers.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Mean squared error on raw pixel values.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Absolute error between label strings.

easy.hint: Next step: check what the model outputs: probabilities or numbers.
easy.explanation: Classification needs a loss on class probabilities, canonically cross-entropy.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: digit label is a category, so the model outputs probabilities. Step 2: cross-entropy scores the probability of the true class. Step 3: treating labels 0,1,2 as numbers invents a false ordering. Step 4: pixel reconstruction error ignores the labels entirely.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Label indices are nominal; penalizing index distance is meaningless.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Pixel error trains reconstruction, not classification.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Strings have no numeric error; the loss must score probabilities.

easy.prompt: For spam vs not-spam email labels, why is 0-1-style loss natural?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 0-1 loss counts relevance mistakes; squared error on doc IDs is meaningless.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Squared error on document IDs, since ranking is numeric.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Absolute error on query string length.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Hinge loss on click timestamps.

easy.hint: Next step: identify the true target before picking the loss.
easy.explanation: Match the loss to the target type: classification error for relevance labels.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: the target is relevant vs not, a binary label. Step 2: 0-1 loss counts wrong verdicts. Step 3: document IDs are arbitrary identifiers with no order. Step 4: string length and timestamps are not the prediction target.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: IDs carry no magnitude; squaring their difference is nonsense.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Query length is a feature, not the label to predict.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Timestamps are not the relevance verdict being scored.

easy.prompt: What does linear regression compute on housing size vs price data?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A straight line (or hyperplane) fit by minimizing squared residuals.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A step function fit by counting misclassifications only.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A decision tree grown to full depth.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A clustering of inputs ignoring targets.

easy.hint: Next step: write the prediction formula, then the residual.
easy.explanation: Linear regression fits a linear surface by least squares on residuals.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: model predicts w·x + b, a linear surface. Step 2: residual is y minus prediction per row. Step 3: least squares minimizes the average squared residual. Step 4: counting errors or clustering optimizes something else entirely.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Step rules and 0-1 counts belong to classifiers, not least squares.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Trees partition space; they do not fit one global line.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Clustering ignores y, while regression fits y from x.

easy.prompt: A student claims least squares needs iterative tuning. What is the closed-form fact?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The normal equations solve it in closed form when features are independent.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It has no solution; gradient descent can never be applied.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only a test set can solve for the weights.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Weights must be guessed randomly with no objective.

easy.hint: Next step: set the gradient of squared loss to zero and solve.
easy.explanation: Least squares has a closed-form solution via the normal equations.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: squared loss is convex in w. Step 2: set gradient X'Xw − X'y to zero. Step 3: solve w = (X'X)^{-1}X'y in one shot. Step 4: gradient descent is an alternative route to the same minimum, not the only one.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Both closed form and gradient descent solve it; neither is impossible.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Test data never sets weights; train data does.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Weights optimize a concrete objective, not random guesses.

easy.prompt: Why did one $10M mansion listing tilt the whole price line?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Squared residual per row, averaged; one outlier pulls the line strongly.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Absolute label value per row; outliers have no effect.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Number of features; more features always lower the loss to zero.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Test accuracy; train residuals are irrelevant.

easy.hint: Next step: square one large residual and see its weight in the average.
easy.explanation: Least squares averages squared residuals, so large errors dominate.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: residual r = y − (w·x+b). Step 2: loss averages r². Step 3: a residual of 10 contributes 100, dominating the average. Step 4: that quadratic pull is why one outlier tilts the fitted line.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Loss uses residuals, not raw label magnitudes; outliers matter greatly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Feature count is not the loss; fit quality is.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Train residuals define the objective; test is a separate estimate.

easy.prompt: Logistic regression outputs σ(w·x+b) = 0.8 for an email. What does 0.8 mean?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Squashes any real number into (0,1) as P(y=1|x).

choices.label: B
choices.body: Rounds any input to the nearest integer class.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Outputs only exactly 0 or 1, never in between.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Sorts inputs into three equal bins.

easy.hint: Next step: plug z = 0 into 1/(1+e^{−z}) and interpret the result.
easy.explanation: Sigmoid outputs a probability; the label needs a separate threshold step.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: compute z = w·x + b, any real. Step 2: apply σ(z) = 1/(1+e^{−z}). Step 3: z=0 maps to 0.5, large z nears 1, very negative nears 0. Step 4: the result is a probability; the class comes only after thresholding.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No rounding happens; 0.8 stays 0.8 until you threshold it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Outputs are continuous between 0 and 1, not hard 0/1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Binning is unrelated; sigmoid is a smooth probability map.

easy.prompt: If P(spam|x) = 0.8 and your threshold is 0.9, what is the prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 80% chance of spam; still ham if the threshold is 0.9.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Definitely spam regardless of threshold.

choices.label: C
choices.body: 80 spam words counted in the email.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The model is 80% accurate overall.

easy.hint: Next step: compare the probability against the decision threshold.
easy.explanation: Probability plus threshold gives the label; 0.8 below a 0.9 cutoff predicts ham.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: 0.8 estimates P(spam|x). Step 2: decide spam only if 0.8 exceeds your threshold. Step 3: with threshold 0.9, 0.8 falls short, so predict ham. Step 4: one probability says nothing about overall accuracy or word counts.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Class depends on threshold; 0.8 is not automatically spam.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 0.8 is a probability, not a word count.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Single-example probability is not dataset accuracy.

easy.prompt: What does the sigmoid curve look like, and why does it matter?

choices.label: A
choices.body: An S-curve steep near 0 and flat at extremes, so confident outputs saturate.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A straight line through the origin with constant slope.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A U-shape minimized at zero.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A random scatter with no pattern.

easy.hint: Next step: evaluate σ at −5, 0, and 5 and compare the gaps.
easy.explanation: Sigmoid is S-shaped: sensitive near zero, saturated (flat) when confident.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: near z=0, σ rises steeply (~0.25 slope). Step 2: near z=±5, σ is ~0.993 or ~0.007 and barely moves. Step 3: that flatness is saturation: big z changes move probability little. Step 4: a line or U-shape would not bound outputs to (0,1).

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A line is unbounded; sigmoid is bounded and curved.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: U-shapes grow both ways; sigmoid flattens at both ends.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sigmoid is a fixed smooth formula, not random.

easy.prompt: What is one gradient-descent update for weights w with learning rate η?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Step opposite the gradient: w ← w − η∇L.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Step along the gradient: w ← w + η∇L.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Set weights to the gradient itself: w ← ∇L.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Add a constant to all weights each step.

easy.hint: Next step: ask which direction decreases the loss.
easy.explanation: Gradient descent moves downhill: subtract the scaled gradient.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: gradient points uphill (steepest increase). Step 2: negate it to head downhill. Step 3: scale by learning rate η. Step 4: adding the gradient or copying it would climb or discard position.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Adding the gradient climbs to higher loss.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Copying the gradient forgets the current position.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A blind constant ignores the loss surface entirely.

easy.prompt: Training loss bounces 2.1 → 3.4 → 1.9 → 3.8. What is wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Loss oscillates or diverges; η is too large.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Loss falls smoothly; η is well chosen.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Loss is flat; the model has converged perfectly.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Loss rises slowly; training is proceeding normally.

easy.hint: Next step: connect bouncing steps to step size.
easy.explanation: Oscillating/diverging loss means the learning rate overshoots; shrink it.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: each step should modestly reduce loss. Step 2: bouncing up and down means steps overshoot the valley. Step 3: overshoot grows when η exceeds the stable range. Step 4: smooth falling loss is the healthy pattern, not oscillation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Smooth decrease is healthy; bouncing is not.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Flat loss can mean stuck or converged, not violent bouncing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Rising loss is never normal progress.

easy.prompt: How does learning-rate size affect gradient descent?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Smaller steps converge slowly but stably; larger steps risk overshoot.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Step size has no effect on training.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Larger steps are always safer and faster.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Learning rate only affects the test set.

easy.hint: Next step: picture stepping across a narrow valley.
easy.explanation: Learning rate trades speed (large) against stability (small).
easy.deepDive: Step 1: tiny η creeps downhill needing many steps. Step 2: moderate η descends briskly. Step 3: huge η leaps across the valley and diverges. Step 4: so η trades speed against stability on every problem.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Step size directly scales every update; it matters enormously.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Oversized steps diverge instead of speeding up.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Learning rate shapes training optimization, not test data.

easy.prompt: A linear fit on clearly curved data scores poorly on train and validation. Diagnose in bias-variance terms?

choices.label: A
choices.body: High bias, low variance: too rigid to capture signal, stable across samples.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Low bias, high variance: captures signal but swings wildly.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Low bias, low variance: the ideal model.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Zero bias and zero noise always.

easy.hint: Next step: ask whether errors are systematic or jittery across samples.
easy.explanation: Underfitting means systematic miss (high bias) with stable fits (low variance).
easy.deepDive: Step 1: a line on curved data misses systematically (bias). Step 2: refits on new samples barely move the line (low variance). Step 3: train and validation errors are both high and close. Step 4: the flexible memorizer shows the opposite pattern.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That pattern is overfitting: good train, bad validation with jitter.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Ideal models fit well; this one fits poorly everywhere.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Irreducible noise never vanishes; zero-zero is impossible.

easy.prompt: A deep tree hits 99% train but 70% validation. Diagnose in bias-variance terms?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Low bias, high variance: nails train, fails validation, jitters across samples.

choices.label: B
choices.body: High bias, low variance.

choices.label: C
choices.body: High bias, high variance always.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No bias and no variance.

easy.hint: Next step: compare train vs validation and imagine refitting on new data.
easy.explanation: Overfitting is low bias on train plus high variance across samples.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: deep tree hits 99% train, 70% validation. Step 2: the 29-point gap shows memorization. Step 3: new samples reshape the jagged boundary (variance). Step 4: systematic-miss models instead err equally on both splits.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: High bias would depress train too; here train shines.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Overfit is specifically low train bias with high variance, not high-high.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Variance never vanishes for flexible fits on finite samples.

easy.prompt: What is the bias-variance decomposition for squared loss?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Expected squared error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Expected error = bias × variance + noise.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Expected error = bias only.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Expected error = variance squared plus noise squared.

easy.hint: Next step: recall which term is squared and how they combine.
easy.explanation: Squared-loss error decomposes additively into three named parts.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: bias² measures systematic miss of the average model. Step 2: variance measures jitter around that average. Step 3: noise σ² is label randomness no model removes. Step 4: the three add; they do not multiply or square together.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Terms add; only bias is squared.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Variance and noise are missing from this account.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Only bias is squared; variance and noise enter linearly.

easy.prompt: During training, when do learning curves signal overfitting?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Falling train loss with rising validation loss: stop, it memorizes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Both losses falling: stop immediately, it overfits.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Both losses high and flat: the model overfits.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Validation below train: clear overfitting.

easy.hint: Next step: check whether the two curves move in opposite directions.
easy.explanation: Diverging curves (train down, validation up) are the overfit signature.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: plot loss vs epochs. Step 2: train keeps improving while validation turns upward. Step 3: the turning point is where memorization overtakes learning. Step 4: jointly falling curves mean healthy learning; jointly high means underfit.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Jointly falling means generalization still improves; continue.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Jointly high and flat means underfit, not memorization.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Validation below train is unusual luck, not the overfit pattern.

easy.prompt: Train error 25% and validation 26%, both flat. What does that mean?

choices.label: A
choices.body: High flat train and validation error: too simple or undertrained.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Low train with high validation: too simple.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Low train with low validation: too simple.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Curves can never diagnose capacity problems.

easy.hint: Next step: ask whether train itself is already bad.
easy.explanation: Jointly high errors with a small gap mean underfit, not overfit.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: train error 25%, validation 26%, both stuck. Step 2: the model cannot even fit train, so capacity or training is lacking. Step 3: the tiny gap rules out memorization. Step 4: low-train/high-val would instead indict excess capacity.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That split pattern is overfitting, the opposite diagnosis.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Jointly low means success, not simplicity failure.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Curve shapes are the standard capacity diagnostic.

easy.prompt: What does a widening train-validation gap late in training tell you?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Widening train-validation gap late in training: memorize phase; consider stopping.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Narrowing gap with both falling: memorize phase.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Gap size is meaningless for model selection.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Only the final epoch matters, never the curves.

easy.hint: Next step: watch the gap width as epochs advance.
easy.explanation: A growing gap late in training tracks memorization overtaking learning.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: early epochs shrink both errors. Step 2: later, train keeps shrinking but validation grows. Step 3: the gap width tracks memorization directly. Step 4: narrowing jointly-falling gaps instead show healthy convergence.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Narrowing jointly-falling gaps show improving generalization.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Gap width is the core memorization meter.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Curve history locates the turning point; the endpoint alone hides it.

easy.prompt: What does cross-validation give you that a single train/test split does not?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A lower-variance estimate of new-data performance than one split.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A faster training loop than one split.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A guarantee against overfitting.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A larger model with more parameters.

easy.hint: Next step: ask what averaging does to a noisy estimate.
easy.explanation: Cross-validation averages splits to stabilize the performance estimate.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: one split's estimate depends on its lucky rows. Step 2: 5-fold averages 5 such estimates over different held-out rows. Step 3: averaging cuts the variance of the estimate. Step 4: it costs 5× training and still only estimates; it prevents nothing by itself.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: CV trains k times, so it is slower, not faster.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: It measures overfitting; restraint and capacity fix it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Model size is unchanged; only the evaluation repeats.

easy.prompt: When is cross-validation most valuable?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Small data where one split's luck dominates the estimate.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Huge data where one split is already stable.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Cases where training is impossibly slow.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Cases where you need a bigger model.

easy.hint: Next step: compare validation size to the noise of the estimate.
easy.explanation: CV pays off most when single-split estimates are noisy: small data.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: with 200 rows, one 40-row validation is noisy. Step 2: reshuffling changes the winner by luck. Step 3: averaging 5 folds pools 200 held-out verdicts. Step 4: with 2M rows, one 400k validation is already rock solid.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Huge validation sets are already stable; CV adds little.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Slow training makes k× cost hurt more, not less.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: CV evaluates models; it does not enlarge them.

easy.prompt: A teammate says cross-validation stops overfitting by itself. What is wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It estimates performance honestly but does not itself prevent memorization.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It shrinks model capacity automatically.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It adds training data automatically.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It tunes the learning rate by itself.

easy.hint: Next step: separate measuring from intervening.
easy.explanation: CV is a meter, not a fix: it reveals overfitting without curing it.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: CV scores each setting on held-out folds. Step 2: you still must choose the simpler winner yourself. Step 3: the scores only reveal which memorizes. Step 4: capacity, data, and penalties do the preventing.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Capacity is set by you; CV only scores the options.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Folds reuse the same rows; no new data appears.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Learning rates need their own search; CV just evaluates.

easy.prompt: How does a classification tree choose its next split?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Pick the split that most reduces impurity (e.g. Gini), recursing on each child.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Split randomly without measuring label separation.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Split to balance row counts ignoring labels.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Split each feature exactly once at its mean.

easy.hint: Next step: compute impurity before and after a candidate split.
easy.explanation: Greedy impurity reduction picks each split; the biggest drop wins.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: measure parent impurity, e.g. Gini 0.5 on 50/50. Step 2: try each feature/threshold, compute weighted child impurity. Step 3: keep the split with the biggest drop. Step 4: recurse; label-blind rules cannot find separation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Random splits ignore the labels the tree must separate.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Balanced counts without label purity can separate nothing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: One fixed mean-split per feature misses better thresholds.

easy.prompt: Node X is 50/50, node Y is 90/10. Which is purer by Gini impurity?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Gini 0.5 on 50/50 vs 0.18 on 90/10: purer child has lower Gini.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Gini is higher for purer nodes.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Gini ignores class mix entirely.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Gini equals accuracy in every node.

easy.hint: Next step: compute 1 − (p² + (1−p)²) for each mix.
easy.explanation: Gini falls as purity rises: 0.5 for even splits, near 0 for pure nodes.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: Gini = 1 − Σ p². Step 2: 50/50 gives 1 − (0.25+0.25) = 0.5. Step 3: 90/10 gives 1 − (0.81+0.01) = 0.18. Step 4: lower means purer; higher-mix nodes score higher.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Reversed: impurity peaks at even mixes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Class mix is exactly what Gini measures.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Gini is an impurity score, not the accuracy rate.

easy.prompt: How does a tree split a numeric feature like age?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Thresholds turn numbers into yes/no questions, e.g. age < 30.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Numbers enter trees only as raw sums.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Trees cannot use numeric features at all.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Numeric splits always use the feature mean.

easy.hint: Next step: sort the values and try midpoints.
easy.explanation: Numeric features split at searched thresholds forming binary questions.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: sort rows by age. Step 2: try midpoints between consecutive values. Step 3: score each by impurity drop. Step 4: keep age < 30 if it separates best; sums and mean-only rules skip this search.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Trees branch on comparisons, not weighted sums.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Threshold search is the standard numeric handler.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The mean is one candidate; the best midpoint wins.

easy.prompt: What happens when a decision tree grows to unlimited depth?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Unlimited depth memorizes: 100% train, weak validation.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Unlimited depth generalizes best because train is perfect.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Depth never affects generalization.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Shallow trees always overfit more than deep ones.

easy.hint: Next step: ask what a leaf with one row predicts on new data.
easy.explanation: Unbounded depth memorizes train rows and fails on new rows.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: deep leaves isolate single rows. Step 2: train hits ~100% by memorization. Step 3: new rows land in arbitrary single-row leaves. Step 4: validation drops while the gap balloons.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Train-perfect is memorization's signature, not proof of skill.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Depth is the capacity knob of trees.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Reversed: shallowness underfits; depth overfits.

easy.prompt: How do you control a tree that overfits?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Cap depth or require min samples per leaf, chosen on validation.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Grow full depth and tune on test until it looks good.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Delete the validation set to save the tree.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Add more features to fix depth memorization.

easy.hint: Next step: limit how finely leaves can carve the data.
easy.explanation: Constrain leaves (depth, min samples) and pick the limit by validation.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: depth caps and min-leaf rules limit leaf count. Step 2: fewer leaves cannot isolate every row. Step 3: validation scores across caps reveal the sweet spot. Step 4: test-tuning or deleting validation hides the meter; features add capacity.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Test-tuning leaks the final judge.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Validation is the meter you need, not dead weight.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Features add capacity, worsening memorization.

easy.prompt: Depth 2: 71%/70%; depth 30: 100%/72% (train/val). Which regime is which?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Depth 2 underfits (both ~70%); depth 30 overfits (100%/72%); prefer the middle.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Depth 30 wins because train is highest.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Depth 2 wins because simplest is always best.

choices.label: D
choices.body: All depths generalize identically.

easy.hint: Next step: label each depth as bias or variance regime.
easy.explanation: Read both ends: underfit stub vs memorized giant, operate in the middle.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: depth 2: train 71%, val 70%, both poor. Step 2: depth 30: train 100%, val 72%, big gap. Step 3: the middle (say depth 8: 88%/85%) balances. Step 4: train-best and simplest-only rules each ignore half the tradeoff.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Train-best depth is memorization, exposed by validation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Simplest is not best when the middle validates higher.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Depth moves the tradeoff from 70% to 85% validation here.

easy.prompt: What is bagging for decision trees?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Train many trees on bootstrap samples and average (or vote) them.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Train one tree on the full data with no resampling.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Train trees sequentially, each fixing prior errors.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Average the raw features before training one tree.

easy.hint: Next step: ask whether trees train in parallel on resamples or in sequence on errors.
easy.explanation: Bagging averages bootstrapped trees to calm their variance.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: draw n rows with replacement per tree. Step 2: fit a tree on each resample. Step 3: average predictions (vote for classes). Step 4: single-tree and sequential-error-fixing describe other methods.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: One tree is the un-bagged baseline with full variance.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Sequential error-fixing is boosting, not bagging.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Averaging inputs is not bootstrap aggregation of models.

easy.prompt: Why does bagging help wiggly deep trees?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Averaging cancels uncorrelated errors, cutting variance.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Averaging removes all bias automatically.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Averaging compresses trees into one small model.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Averaging eliminates the need for training data.

easy.hint: Next step: ask which error term averaging acts on.
easy.explanation: Bagging's averaging trims variance; bias barely moves.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: each deep tree jitters with its sample. Step 2: jitters partly cancel when averaged. Step 3: variance falls while bias stays similar. Step 4: the ensemble is bigger, not smaller, and still needs data.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Bias falls only if errors point in different systematic ways.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Ensembles grow total size; they do not compress.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Every tree still trains on resampled data.

easy.prompt: What is a bootstrap sample, and what are out-of-bag rows?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Bootstrap resamples with replacement: some rows repeat, ~37% are left out.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Bootstrap means splitting off the test set.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Bootstrap means sorting rows by label.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Bootstrap means deleting outliers.

easy.hint: Next step: compute the chance one row is never picked.
easy.explanation: Bootstraps resample with replacement, leaving ~37% out-of-bag per tree.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: draw n picks with replacement from n rows. Step 2: repeats occur; P(row never picked) ≈ (1−1/n)^n ≈ 1/e ≈ 37%. Step 3: those out-of-bag rows validate that tree honestly. Step 4: test-splitting, sorting, and deleting describe other steps.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Test splitting quarantines final data; bootstraps feed training.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Sorting is not resampling.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No rows are deleted; they are reweighted by sampling.

easy.prompt: What is the margin of a linear classifier?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The gap between the classes' boundary lines; SVM maximizes it.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The number of support vectors in the dataset.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The learning rate used in training.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The count of misclassified points.

easy.hint: Next step: draw the two bounding lines and measure their gap.
easy.explanation: Margin is the empty street between classes; wider means more confident separation.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: parallel lines bound each class at distance. Step 2: margin width = 2/||w||. Step 3: maximizing width minimizes ||w||. Step 4: counts, rates, and errors are different quantities entirely.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Support-vector count results from the margin, it is not the margin.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Learning rate is an optimizer setting, not a geometric gap.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Error counts ignore the distance geometry.

easy.prompt: Why does maximizing the margin help generalization?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Larger margin usually means better new-data separation.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Larger margin always guarantees zero test error.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Margin size has no link to generalization.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Smaller margins always generalize better.

easy.hint: Next step: perturb a test point slightly and see which street holds.
easy.explanation: Wider margins tolerate perturbation, aiding generalization (no guarantees).
easy.deepDive: Step 1: margin 0.1 vs 1.0 on separable train. Step 2: the wider street tolerates more jitter in new points. Step 3: theory bounds error by margin size. Step 4: guarantees of zero and smaller-is-better reverse the logic.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No finite sample guarantees zero future error.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Margin bounds are a core generalization result.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Tighter streets shatter sooner under noise.

easy.prompt: For a separable SVM with weight norm ||w|| = 2, what is the margin width?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Margin = 2/||w||, so doubling ||w|| halves the margin.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Margin = ||w||, so doubling ||w|| doubles the margin.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Margin is independent of ||w||.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Margin equals the bias term b.

easy.hint: Next step: compute distance from the line to a support point.
easy.explanation: Minimizing ||w|| maximizes margin via the 2/||w|| formula.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: constraints y(w·x+b) ≥ 1 fix the scale. Step 2: distance from line to support = 1/||w||. Step 3: two sides give 2/||w||. Step 4: ||w||=2 gives margin 1; ||w||=4 gives 0.5.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Inverted formula: bigger weights mean a narrower street.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Norm directly sets street width under the unit constraint.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: b shifts the line; width comes from w.

easy.prompt: Which training points are the support vectors?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The training points lying exactly on the margin boundary.

choices.label: B
choices.body: All training points equally.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only the misclassified points.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Randomly chosen test points.

easy.hint: Next step: ask which rows the boundary rests on.
easy.explanation: Support vectors are the boundary-hugging rows that determine the line.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: constraints y(w·x+b) ≥ 1 bind tightly for some rows. Step 2: those boundary rows pin the solution. Step 3: moving an interior row changes nothing. Step 4: misclassified-only and test-based picks miss the boundary definition.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Interior points sit strictly inside and do not bind the solution.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Misclassified points matter in soft-margin, but boundary points define it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Support vectors are training rows, never test rows.

easy.prompt: What happens if you delete training rows that are not support vectors?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Deleting non-support rows leaves the boundary unchanged.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Deleting any single row always changes the boundary.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Support vectors can be deleted with no effect.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The boundary depends on test points.

easy.hint: Next step: refit after removing an interior row.
easy.explanation: Only support vectors bind the solution; interior rows are inert.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: fit SVM, note the 3 boundary supports. Step 2: remove 50 interior rows, refit. Step 3: constraints unchanged, same w and b. Step 4: removing a support instead shifts the street; test rows never enter fitting.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Interior rows are slack; their removal changes nothing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Reversed: supports are exactly the load-bearing rows.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Test data never participates in fitting.

easy.prompt: With 1000 training rows but 12 support vectors, what does that imply?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Few supports relative to n: sparse, boundary-local solution.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Every row is always a support vector.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Support count equals feature count always.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Support count grows with test size.

easy.hint: Next step: count which rows actually enter the prediction sum.
easy.explanation: SVM solutions are sparse: few boundary rows carry the whole model.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: 1000 rows, 12 supports on the street edges. Step 2: the line is fixed by those 12. Step 3: prediction sums over supports only, hence sparse. Step 4: all-rows and feature-count rules are false; test plays no role.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Interior rows rarely bind; all-rows is atypical.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Support count reflects geometry, not dimensionality.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Test size cannot change a fitted training solution.

easy.prompt: What does increasing C do in a soft-margin SVM?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Large C punishes slack: narrower margin, fewer violations.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Large C widens the margin and allows more violations.

choices.label: C
choices.body: C has no effect on the fit.

choices.label: D
choices.body: C sets the learning rate.

easy.hint: Next step: ask what a bigger violation price buys.
easy.explanation: C prices margin violations: big C obeys data, small C favors wide streets.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: objective = ||w||²/2 + C·Σ slack. Step 2: big C prices violations steeply. Step 3: the optimizer narrows the street to obey rows. Step 4: small C instead buys a wide street with tolerated violations.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Reversed: strictness narrows the street and cuts violations.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: C directly scales the slack penalty term.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Learning rate is separate from the C tradeoff.

easy.prompt: C=1000 gives train 100%/val 75%; C=0.01 gives 90%/87%. Which C and why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: C=0.01 (wide street, some errors) beats C=1000 (jagged overfit) on validation.

choices.label: B
choices.body: C=1000 always generalizes best because train is cleanest.

choices.label: C
choices.body: C choice never changes validation scores.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Always pick the largest C available.

easy.hint: Next step: rank C values by validation, not train.
easy.explanation: Validate C: strict fits memorize outliers, gentle ones generalize.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: C=1000: train 100%, val 75%, jagged street threading outliers. Step 2: C=0.01: train 90%, val 87%, smooth street. Step 3: validation favors the smoother tradeoff. Step 4: train-cleanest and always-max rules pick memorization.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Train-cleanest here is outlier memorization.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: C moves the bias-variance tradeoff decisively.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Unbounded strictness overfits; validation must cap it.

easy.prompt: A teammate sets C=10⁶ 'to be safe'. What is wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.body: More C is not always better; validate it like any capacity knob.

choices.label: B
choices.body: More C always improves test accuracy.

choices.label: C
choices.body: C only affects training speed.

choices.label: D
choices.body: C must equal the number of features.

easy.hint: Next step: sketch validation versus C.
easy.explanation: C is a regularizer in disguise: tune it, do not max it.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: sweep C over 0.001…1000. Step 2: validation traces a U: underfit, sweet spot, overfit. Step 3: the peak sits in the middle. Step 4: monotonic-more and speed-only myths ignore the U.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Huge C overfits outliers; test falls past the sweet spot.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: C sets the fit tradeoff, not the clock.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: C is a penalty price with no link to dimensionality.

easy.prompt: What objective does k-means optimize, and how?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Minimize within-cluster squared distance to assigned centroids, alternating assignment and update.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Maximize the distance between all pairs of points.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Count the true number of clusters automatically.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Sort points by label and split evenly.

easy.hint: Next step: ask what two steps repeat until centroids stop moving.
easy.explanation: K-means alternates nearest-centroid assignment with mean recomputation to cut within-cluster variance.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: assign each point to its nearest centroid. Step 2: move each centroid to its members' mean. Step 3: repeat; the squared-error objective falls each round. Step 4: pair-spreading, auto-k, and even-splitting describe other things.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: K-means compacts clusters; spreading pairs is the opposite.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: K is an input you choose, not discovered by the algorithm.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Labels are unknown in clustering; even splits ignore geometry.

easy.prompt: How is k-means initialized, and why run it several times?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Random points as initial centroids; different starts can give different clusters.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The true cluster labels as initialization.

choices.label: C
choices.body: All centroids stacked at one location always.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No initialization is needed; k-means is deterministic.

easy.hint: Next step: ask where the first centroids come from.
easy.explanation: Random starts plus local optima mean k-means needs multiple restarts.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: pick k starting centroids at random. Step 2: iterate assignment and update to a local minimum. Step 3: rerun with new seeds; scores differ across runs. Step 4: true labels are unavailable, stacking collapses clusters, determinism is false.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Labels are exactly what clustering lacks.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Coincident starts waste centroids and trap the fit.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Random starts make runs differ; best-of-N is standard.

easy.prompt: In one k-means iteration, how are points reassigned?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each point goes to its nearest centroid by Euclidean distance.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Each point joins the largest cluster regardless of distance.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Points are assigned randomly each round.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Points join clusters to balance sizes exactly.

easy.hint: Next step: compare the point's distance to each centroid.
easy.explanation: Assignment is nearest-centroid; that step greedily improves the objective.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: compute distances from the point to all k centroids. Step 2: attach it to the argmin. Step 3: this greedy step lowers the squared-error objective. Step 4: size-based or random rules ignore the distance objective.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Size-chasing ignores the distance objective.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Random assignment would raise, not lower, the objective.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Balanced sizes are not the k-means goal.

easy.prompt: Does k-means find the true number of clusters automatically?

choices.label: A
choices.body: K is a chosen setting; validate it with elbow, silhouette, or task scores.

choices.label: B
choices.body: K-means discovers the true k by itself from data.

choices.label: C
choices.body: K must always equal the feature count.

choices.label: D
choices.body: K must always equal 2 regardless of data.

easy.hint: Next step: ask which input the algorithm requires before starting.
easy.explanation: K is a hyperparameter: compare candidates with elbow/silhouette/task metrics.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: run k = 2…8, record within-cluster error. Step 2: error falls steeply then flattens (elbow). Step 3: silhouette peaks near natural group counts. Step 4: no internal statistic reveals metaphysical truth; k stays a choice.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The core misconception: k is an input, never an output.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Features and clusters are unrelated counts.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Two is one candidate, not a law.

easy.prompt: How do you read an elbow plot for choosing k?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Plot within-cluster error vs k; pick the bend where returns diminish.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Pick the k with the largest within-cluster error.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Always pick k = n (one cluster per point).

choices.label: D
choices.body: Elbow plots need labeled test data.

easy.hint: Next step: compare marginal error drops as k grows.
easy.explanation: The elbow's bend marks where extra clusters stop paying off.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: k=1: error 100; k=2: 40; k=3: 32; k=4: 28. Step 2: the 100→40 drop dwarfs later gains. Step 3: the bend at k=2 marks diminishing returns. Step 4: max-error and k=n rules invert the logic; labels are unnecessary.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Largest error is the worst fit, not the best k.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: k=n gives zero error but zero insight: pure memorization.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Elbow uses unsupervised error only; labels are not needed.

easy.prompt: What does a silhouette score tell you about a clustering?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Silhouette near 1: tight fit, far neighbors; near 0/negative: overlapping or misassigned.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Silhouette is always exactly 1 for any clustering.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Higher k always raises silhouette to 1.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Silhouette measures accuracy against true labels.

easy.hint: Next step: compare distance to own cluster vs nearest other cluster.
easy.explanation: Silhouette contrasts cohesion with separation per point, averaged overall.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: a = mean intra-cluster distance, b = nearest-cluster distance. Step 2: s = (b−a)/max(a,b). Step 3: a≪b gives s≈1 (great); a≈b gives s≈0 (overlap). Step 4: constants, monotonic-k, and accuracy claims misread the formula.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Scores span −1…1 and vary by point.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Fragmenting clusters can lower silhouette; monotonic rise is false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Silhouette is label-free; accuracy needs ground truth.

easy.prompt: What does a 2×2 confusion matrix show?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Rows = actual classes, columns = predicted: TP, FP, FN, TN cells.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Rows = features, columns = weights of the model.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A plot of loss versus epochs.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A table of cluster centroids.

easy.hint: Next step: place one prediction by its actual and predicted labels.
easy.explanation: Confusion matrices cross-tabulate actual vs predicted classes.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: actual positive, predicted positive → TP cell. Step 2: actual negative, predicted positive → FP cell. Step 3: the four cells tally every verdict type. Step 4: weights, loss curves, and centroids are different artifacts.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Weights live in parameter vectors, not verdict tables.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Loss curves track training, not verdict types.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Centroids belong to clustering, not classification tallies.

easy.prompt: A spam filter flags 50 emails; 40 are truly spam. What is precision?

choices.label: A
choices.body: TP=40, FP=10: precision = 40/50 = 80%.

choices.label: B
choices.body: TP=40, FP=10: precision = 40/100.

choices.label: C
choices.body: TP=40, FP=10: precision = 10/40.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Precision uses only FN and TN.

easy.hint: Next step: count how many positives the model predicted in total.
easy.explanation: Precision divides true positives by all predicted positives.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: predicted positives = TP + FP = 50. Step 2: correct among them = TP = 40. Step 3: 40/50 = 0.8. Step 4: denominators of all actuals or inverted ratios answer other questions.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 100 is not the predicted-positive count; 50 is.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Inverted ratio gives FP/TP, not precision.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: FN/TN belong to recall and specificity, not precision.

easy.prompt: 50 spam emails exist; the filter catches 40. What is recall?

choices.label: C
choices.body: Recall uses FP instead of FN.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Recall equals the false-positive rate.

easy.hint: Next step: count how many positives truly existed.
easy.explanation: Recall divides recovered positives by all actual positives.
easy.deepDive: Step 1: actual positives = TP + FN = 50. Step 2: recovered = TP = 40. Step 3: 40/50 = 0.8. Step 4: FP-based or FPR readings answer precision-type questions instead.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 100 is not the actual-positive count; 50 is.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: FP belongs to precision, not recall.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: FPR = FP/(FP+TN); recall = TP/(TP+FN).

medium.prompt: What is empirical risk, and what does ERM do with it?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The average loss on the training set for a candidate model.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The average loss on the test set for a candidate model.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The worst-case loss over all possible models.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The loss on a single hardest example.

medium.hint: Next step: replace the unknowable expectation with the computable sample average.
medium.explanation: Empirical risk is training-average loss; ERM picks its minimizer.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: risk is expected loss over the true distribution. Step 2: we cannot compute it, so we substitute the training average. Step 3: ERM picks the model minimizing that training average. Step 4: test loss instead estimates risk after selection; worst-case is a different robust objective.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Test average estimates risk after the fact; ERM optimizes the train average.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Worst-case over models is not an average over data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: One example is not an average; ERM averages over all n train points.

medium.prompt: Linear regression via least squares is ERM with which objective?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Minimize average loss on the collected training sample.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Minimize loss on the test set directly.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Maximize the margin on validation data.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Minimize the number of features regardless of loss.

medium.hint: Next step: write the average over the data you are allowed to optimize.
medium.explanation: ERM optimizes the in-sample average as a stand-in for true risk.

medium.prompt: Why is ERM alone not a guarantee of good new-data performance?

choices.label: A
choices.body: ERM can memorize noise, so low train loss need not mean low true risk.

choices.label: B
choices.body: ERM always finds the global optimum of true risk.

choices.label: C
choices.body: ERM ignores the loss function entirely.

choices.label: D
choices.body: ERM requires infinite data to run at all.

medium.hint: Next step: ask whether the average you minimized equals the expectation you care about.
medium.explanation: ERM minimizes a noisy proxy, so memorization can drive train loss below true risk.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: train average is a noisy estimate of true risk. Step 2: a rich model class fits the noise in the sample. Step 3: the minimizer of the noisy estimate can be far from the minimizer of truth. Step 4: that is why validation and capacity control exist alongside ERM.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: ERM sees only the sample, not the true distribution.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: ERM is defined by the loss; it cannot ignore it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: ERM runs on any finite sample; guarantees need data, execution does not.

medium.prompt: A model scores 98% on train and 88% on test. What is the generalization gap?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: Train error minus test error; large positive means memorization.

choices.label: D

medium.hint: Next step: put the optimistic number second in the subtraction.
medium.explanation: Generalization gap is test-minus-train; a big positive gap flags overfitting.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: compute train error, e.g. 2%. Step 2: compute test error, e.g. 12%. Step 3: gap = 12 minus 2 = 10 points of optimism. Step 4: reversing the subtraction would report negative 10, hiding the problem.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Reversed subtraction gives -10, which mislabels memorization as good.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Summing errors mixes the level with the gap; gap is a difference.

medium.prompt: Train error 5%, test error 30%. How large is the gap and what does it mean?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

medium.explanation: Subtract train from test: 25 points of gap means the model memorized.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: train error 5%, test error 30%. Step 2: gap = 30 - 5 = 25 points. Step 3: 25 points of optimism with tiny train error is textbook memorization. Step 4: 5 points would need test near 10%, not 30%.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 5 points would require test near 10%; here test is 30%.

medium.prompt: Your image model has a 20-point generalization gap. What should you do?

medium.explanation: A large gap calls for less capacity or more data, not for hiding test.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: gap = test minus train, say 20 points. Step 2: simpler models cannot memorize as much, lowering test while raising train slightly. Step 3: more data also constrains memorization. Step 4: deleting test or tuning on it hides the measurement instead of fixing the model.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A wider gap is more memorization, never the goal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Removing test destroys measurement without improving the model.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Tuning on test leaks it and fakes a small gap.

medium.prompt: Which preprocessing pipeline leaks test information?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.body: Evaluating the frozen model once on test.

medium.explanation: Preprocessing on pooled data leaks test into train features.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: test rows contribute to the vocabulary means. Step 2: train features now encode test information. Step 3: test is no longer unseen, so its score is optimistic. Step 4: fitting stats on train only keeps test quarantined.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Train-only statistics applied downstream is the correct leak-free pattern.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Splitting before fitting is exactly the safe order.

medium.explanation: Duplicate entities across splits let the model memorize instead of generalize.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: ID-grouped splitting is the fix, not the leak.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Train-only standardization is the safe practice.

medium.prompt: What is the leak-free protocol for choosing between 3 model types?

choices.label: A

medium.explanation: Split first, fit on train, select on validation, evaluate once on test.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Training on test contaminates everything downstream.

medium.prompt: Which workflow correctly combines cross-validation with a final test?

choices.label: A

medium.explanation: Rank by cross-validation, refit the winner on train+val, then test once.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: cross-validation averages held-out folds, an honest ranking signal. Step 2: retraining the winner on train+val uses more data after selection. Step 3: the single test pass stays unbiased because choices are frozen. Step 4: picking by train or peeking at test biases selection.

medium.prompt: Which feature-selection workflow leaks into cross-validation?

medium.deepDive: Step 1: feature selection sees all rows' labels. Step 2: folds then validate models built from pre-leaked features. Step 3: scores look better than true new-data performance. Step 4: redoing selection inside each fold quarantines each held-out fold.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: In-fold selection is the correct quarantined pattern.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Holding out test before anything is safe, not leaky.

medium.prompt: What is cross-entropy loss for one labeled example?

choices.label: A
choices.body: −log of the predicted probability of the true class.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.body: Absolute difference of raw logits.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Count of correct predictions.

medium.hint: Next step: ask what score the true class's probability gets.
medium.explanation: Cross-entropy is negative log-likelihood of the true class.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: model gives P(true class) = p. Step 2: loss = −log p. Step 3: p=0.9 gives loss ~0.11; p=0.1 gives ~2.3. Step 4: confident wrong answers are punished far more than mild ones.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Class indices are nominal; their numeric gaps are meaningless.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Logits need probability mapping first; raw gaps are not the loss.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Counts are metrics, not the per-example differentiable loss.

medium.prompt: Why prefer cross-entropy over MSE for logistic regression?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It punishes confident wrong probabilities severely, giving strong corrective gradients.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It runs faster on GPUs than any other loss.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It guarantees calibrated probabilities automatically.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It works without any gradients.

medium.hint: Next step: compare gradient size when confidently wrong under each loss.
medium.explanation: Cross-entropy keeps gradients alive for confident errors, unlike MSE on sigmoids.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: with sigmoid + MSE, confident-wrong regions have near-zero slope. Step 2: with cross-entropy, gradient vs logits is simply (p − y). Step 3: predicting 0.99 for the wrong class gives gradient ~1, a loud correction. Step 4: speed and auto-calibration are myths; the gradient shape is the real reason.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Compute cost is similar; optimization shape is the reason.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Calibration needs extra work; cross-entropy alone does not guarantee it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Cross-entropy is trained with gradients like other losses.

medium.prompt: True label is positive. Compare loss when the model says p=0.9 vs p=0.1.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Loss ≈ 2.3 for p=0.1 vs ≈0.1 for p=0.9: confident errors cost ~20× more.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Both cost the same: loss is symmetric in confidence.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Confident errors cost less than mild ones.

choices.label: D

medium.hint: Next step: compute −log(p) for p = 0.9 and p = 0.1.
medium.explanation: Work the logs: confident-wrong costs an order of magnitude more.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: −log(0.9) ≈ 0.105. Step 2: −log(0.1) ≈ 2.303. Step 3: ratio ≈ 22×. Step 4: the log curve steeply penalizes near-zero probability on the truth.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The log makes costs highly asymmetric in confidence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Reversed: near-zero truth-probability explodes the loss.

medium.prompt: How do L1 and L2 regularization differ in the weights they produce?

choices.label: A
choices.body: L1 drives some weights to exactly 0; L2 shrinks all weights but keeps them nonzero.

choices.label: B
choices.body: L2 drives weights to exactly 0; L1 only shrinks them slightly.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Both always produce identical weight vectors.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Neither affects the weights at all.

medium.hint: Next step: compare the penalty shape at zero: corner vs smooth bowl.
medium.explanation: L1 sparsifies (exact zeros); L2 shrinks smoothly toward zero.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: L1 penalty λΣ|w| has a corner at 0, trapping optima there. Step 2: L2 penalty λΣw² has smooth slope 2λw, approaching but rarely hitting 0. Step 3: so L1 selects features by zeroing, L2 shrinks evenly. Step 4: swapping the roles misstates the geometry.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Reversed: sparsity is the L1 signature, not L2.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Geometries differ, so solutions differ except in edge cases.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Both add penalty terms that directly move the optimum.

medium.prompt: After training, 40 of 100 weights are exactly zero. Which penalty did that?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

medium.hint: Next step: look for literal zeros versus merely small values.
medium.explanation: Exact zeros in the vector signal L1; uniform shrinkage signals L2.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: inspect the weight vector after training. Step 2: exact zeros are the L1 fingerprint. Step 3: uniform shrinkage without zeros is the L2 fingerprint. Step 4: larger weights or LR changes are unrelated to the penalty.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No zeros means L2-style shrinkage, not L1 selection.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Penalties shrink weights; growth contradicts regularization.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Learning rate is an optimizer setting, not a penalty signature.

medium.prompt: Why is L1 called a feature selector?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.body: It squares the weights to grow them.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It adds noise to the inputs.

medium.hint: Next step: ask what a zero weight does to its feature.
medium.explanation: L1 zeros weak weights, using only the surviving features.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: L1 pushes weak features' weights to exactly 0. Step 2: zero-weight features drop out of predictions. Step 3: the surviving nonzero set is the selected subset. Step 4: speed, squaring, and input noise describe other techniques.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Speed is not the distinguishing trait of L1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Squaring describes L2, the opposite penalty.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Input noise is augmentation, not L1.

medium.prompt: What happens as L2 strength λ grows from 0 to very large?

choices.label: A

medium.explanation: More λ means more shrinkage: helpful first, then underfitting.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: small λ gently restrains weights, cutting variance. Step 2: validation error falls as memorization drops. Step 3: huge λ crushes even useful weights toward 0. Step 4: then both train and validation worsen: underfitting.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Penalties shrink weights and first lower validation error, not raise train.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: λ directly scales the penalty term; it always matters.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Exact zeros are the L1 signature, not L2.

medium.prompt: Which underfits less: L2 with λ=0.001 or λ=100?

choices.label: A
choices.body: λ=0.001 underfits less: tiny penalty barely moves weights.

choices.label: B
choices.body: λ=100 underfits less than λ=0.001.

medium.explanation: Small λ barely regularizes; huge λ flattens the model into underfit.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: λ=0.001 adds a whisper of penalty. Step 2: weights stay near unregularized values. Step 3: λ=100 dominates the loss, forcing weights near 0. Step 4: near-zero weights underfit badly, so the tiny λ underfits less.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Reversed: λ=100 crushes weights far more.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Penalty scale changes the optimum continuously.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: λ scales the penalty term, not the optimizer step.

medium.prompt: How should you pick the regularization strength λ in practice?

choices.label: A

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: One constant cannot suit all noise levels and sizes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Train loss always prefers λ=0; it cannot select restraint.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Optimal λ depends on your data scale and noise.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Penalizing b shrinks the global baseline needlessly.

medium.prompt: How does gradient boosting build its ensemble?

choices.label: A

medium.hint: Next step: ask what the next tree's target is.
medium.explanation: Boosting builds additively: each tree fits what remains wrong.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: fit tree 1, compute residuals y − F(x). Step 2: fit tree 2 to those residuals. Step 3: add it with shrinkage: F += η·tree2. Step 4: repeat; parallel averaging is bagging, not this sequential fix-up.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Parallel bootstrap averaging is bagging/RF.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: One tree is the starting point, not the ensemble.

medium.prompt: In AdaBoost, what happens to misclassified examples' weights?

medium.explanation: AdaBoost upweights mistakes so successors prioritize them.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: round 1 misses hard emails. Step 2: AdaBoost raises their weights. Step 3: round 2 optimizes the weighted loss, focusing on those. Step 4: deleting or freezing weights would hide the hard cases instead.

medium.prompt: What are typical gradient-boosting settings that avoid overfitting?

medium.deepDive: Step 1: update F += η·tree with small η like 0.05. Step 2: shallow trees add simple corrections. Step 3: validation picks rounds and η before overfit. Step 4: η=1 with deep trees overshoots and memorizes fast.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: One giant step is a single tree, not boosting.

medium.explanation: Importance totals each feature's impurity savings across the forest.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Tree count is forest size, not feature contribution.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Averages of values ignore label separation entirely.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Units are arbitrary scales, not usefulness.

medium.prompt: Why does tree correlation limit bagging's variance reduction?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Bagging trims variance most when trees disagree; correlated trees average poorly.

choices.label: B

medium.explanation: Bagging gain depends on tree diversity: lower correlation, bigger variance cut.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Identical errors cannot cancel at all.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Copies add no diversity, hence no gain.

choices.label: A

medium.explanation: Hinge keeps rewarding bigger confident margins, unlike 0-1 loss.

medium.prompt: What is the kernel trick?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Compute inner products in a rich feature space via a kernel function, never building the vectors.

medium.deepDive: Step 1: income ~10⁴ vs age ~10¹. Step 2: ||x−z||² is dominated by income gaps. Step 3: age differences vanish from K. Step 4: zero-mean unit-variance scaling balances each axis's vote.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Raw scales let the big axis swallow the small one.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Stretching worsens the domination further.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Distance-based models are the most scale-sensitive of all.

medium.prompt: How do linear SVM and logistic regression differ?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.body: Logistic regression maximizes the margin directly.

choices.label: D
choices.body: SVM outputs calibrated probabilities natively.

medium.hint: Next step: write each model's loss on the same score f.
medium.explanation: Same linear score, different goals: margins vs probabilities.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: linear SVM: hinge on y·f with margin geometry. Step 2: logistic: cross-entropy on σ(f) for probabilities. Step 3: similar linear form f = w·x+b, different objectives. Step 4: identical-loss and native-probability claims blur the distinction.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Hinge vs cross-entropy are different objectives.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Margin maximization is the SVM idea, not logistic's.

medium.prompt: C=0.001 gives train 70%/val 69% (both poor). Diagnose?

medium.explanation: Tiny C underfits: violations are so cheap the street ignores the data.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: tiny C prices violations near zero. Step 2: the optimizer buys a huge street, ignoring many rows. Step 3: train itself scores poorly (70%), so bias dominates. Step 4: the fix is raising C toward the validation peak, not lowering further.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Jagged memorization needs big C, not tiny C.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Jointly poor scores rule out best-generalization claims.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: C sets the fit tradeoff directly, not the clock.

medium.prompt: How does polynomial-kernel degree d affect the SVM boundary?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: Higher degree always generalizes better.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.body: Degree sets the C penalty value.

medium.hint: Next step: picture degree-2 curves versus degree-9 wiggles.
medium.explanation: Polynomial degree is a capacity knob: higher bends more, overfits sooner.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: K = (x·z + c)^d. Step 2: d=2 draws conic curves; d=9 draws wild wiggles. Step 3: wiggles thread train outliers, validation drops. Step 4: always-higher and no-effect myths ignore the capacity knob.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Extreme degrees memorize outliers; better is false.
