medium.prompt: Which formula is precision, and what question does it answer?

choices.label: A
choices.body: TP/(TP+FP): of predicted positives, how many were right.

choices.label: B
choices.body: TP/(TP+FN): of actual positives, how many were found.

choices.label: C
choices.body: (TP+TN)/total: overall correctness.

choices.label: D
choices.body: FP/(FP+TN): false-alarm rate on negatives.

medium.hint: Next step: read which group the denominator describes.
medium.explanation: Precision asks alarm quality; recall asks coverage of actual positives.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: denominator TP+FP = all alarms. Step 2: numerator TP = correct alarms. Step 3: 30/40 = 75% alarm quality. Step 4: the other ratios are recall, accuracy, and FPR respectively.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is recall (coverage), not precision (alarm quality).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is accuracy over everything, not precision.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is the false-positive rate on negatives.

medium.prompt: How do precision and recall move as the decision threshold rises?

choices.label: A
choices.body: High threshold: precision up, recall down; low threshold: the reverse.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Thresholds move precision and recall in the same direction.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Thresholds affect only accuracy, never precision/recall.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Precision and recall are threshold-independent.

medium.hint: Next step: count fired alarms at a high vs low bar.
medium.explanation: The threshold trades alarm purity against coverage; you cannot max both.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: threshold 0.9 fires rarely: alarms pure, many missed. Step 2: precision ≈ 95%, recall ≈ 40%. Step 3: threshold 0.2 fires often: recall ≈ 95%, precision ≈ 50%. Step 4: same-direction and independence myths deny the tradeoff.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: They oppose: purity rises while coverage falls.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Precision/recall are the threshold-sensitive pair.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Both are computed from thresholded labels, so both shift.

medium.prompt: A fraud model has precision 90% but recall 30%. What does that mean?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Precision 90%, recall 30%: pure alarms but misses most positives.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Precision 90%, recall 30%: catches nearly everything.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Precision 90% guarantees accuracy 90%.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Recall 30% means 30% of alarms were wrong.

medium.hint: Next step: reconstruct TP from each rate separately.
medium.explanation: High precision with low recall means trustworthy but sparse alarms.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: 90% of 20 alarms correct = 18 TP. Step 2: 18 of 60 actual positives = 30% recall. Step 3: alarms trustworthy, coverage poor. Step 4: catching-all and accuracy-equality misread the pair; D swaps the definitions.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 30% recall means 70% of frauds missed, not caught.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Accuracy mixes in negatives; equality is false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That 30%-wrong-alarms reading is 1 − precision, not recall.

medium.prompt: What is the F1 score in terms of precision (P) and recall (R)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Harmonic mean of precision and recall: 2PR/(P+R).

choices.label: B
choices.body: Arithmetic mean of precision and recall: (P+R)/2.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Product of accuracy and error rate.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Difference between precision and recall.

medium.hint: Next step: test P=1, R=0.1 under each candidate formula.
medium.explanation: F1 is the harmonic mean, punishing a weak half far more than averaging.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: P=1.0, R=0.1. Step 2: arithmetic mean = 0.55, hiding the failure. Step 3: harmonic = 2·1·0.1/1.1 ≈ 0.18, exposing it. Step 4: harmonics punish lopsided pairs; products and differences are not F1.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Arithmetic mean lets one perfect half mask collapse.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Accuracy-error products are not the F1 definition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Differences ignore the balanced-performance idea.

medium.prompt: Precision = 1.0 but recall = 0.1. What is F1 and what does it reveal?

choices.label: A
choices.body: F1 ≈ 0.18 despite perfect precision: the 0.1 recall dominates.

choices.label: B
choices.body: F1 ≈ 0.55, the simple average of the two.

choices.label: C
choices.body: F1 ≈ 1.0 because precision is perfect.

choices.label: D
choices.body: F1 is undefined whenever precision differs from recall.

medium.hint: Next step: plug into 2PR/(P+R) directly.
medium.explanation: Compute it: F1 hugs the weaker metric, exposing lopsided models.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: 2·1.0·0.1 = 0.2. Step 2: 1.0 + 0.1 = 1.1. Step 3: 0.2/1.1 ≈ 0.18. Step 4: the harmonic stays near the smaller value; averages and perfection claims hide it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 0.55 is the arithmetic mean, not F1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Perfection on one half never suffices for F1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: F1 is defined for any P, R (not both zero).

medium.prompt: Fraud is 1% of rows. Why prefer F1 over accuracy?

choices.label: A
choices.body: F1 balances both; accuracy is swamped by the 99% negatives.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Accuracy, because 99% looks impressive and suffices.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Training loss, because it is the smallest number.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No metric is needed for imbalanced tasks.

medium.hint: Next step: score the all-negative classifier under each metric.
medium.explanation: On imbalance, accuracy lies; F1 keeps both error types honest.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: all-negative scores 99% accuracy, F1 = 0. Step 2: accuracy's denominator drowns positives in negatives. Step 3: F1 averages precision and recall on positives only. Step 4: impressive-looking accuracy here is vacuous.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 99% from all-negative catches zero frauds.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Smallest number is not a validity criterion.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Metrics pick operating points; skipping them flies blind.

medium.prompt: What does an ROC curve plot, and what is AUC?

choices.label: A
choices.body: TPR vs FPR across thresholds; area 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is chance.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Precision vs recall across thresholds.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Loss vs epochs during training.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Accuracy vs batch size.

medium.hint: Next step: ask which rates use actual positives vs actual negatives.
medium.explanation: ROC sweeps thresholds in FPR-TPR space; AUC compresses it to one number.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: sweep threshold 1→0. Step 2: plot (FPR, TPR) points from (0,0) to (1,1). Step 3: perfect model hugs the top-left, area 1.0. Step 4: PR curves, loss curves, and batch plots are different figures.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is a PR curve, a different tradeoff view.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is a training curve, not a threshold sweep.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Batch size never axes an ROC plot.

medium.prompt: AUC = 0.9. What does that mean in plain terms?

choices.label: A
choices.body: P(random positive scores above random negative): ranking quality.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The fraction of correct predictions at threshold 0.5.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The model's training speed in rows per second.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The number of clusters in the data.

medium.hint: Next step: think pairwise comparisons, not one threshold.
medium.explanation: AUC is threshold-free ranking skill: positives above negatives how often.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: pick a random fraud and random legit transaction. Step 2: AUC 0.9 means fraud scores higher 90% of the time. Step 3: this holds across all thresholds at once. Step 4: fixed-threshold accuracy, speed, and cluster counts are different quantities.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is accuracy at one threshold; AUC averages over all.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Speed is unrelated to ranking quality.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Clusters are unsupervised counts, not ranking areas.

medium.prompt: In agglomerative clustering, what do linkage criteria control?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.body: Linkage sets the number of features.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Linkage replaces the distance metric entirely.

medium.hint: Next step: ask how two groups' distance is summarized.
medium.explanation: Linkage rules decide cluster-to-cluster distance, shaping merge order.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: single uses min pair distance (chaining). Step 2: complete uses max pair distance (compact balls). Step 3: average uses mean pairs (compromise). Step 4: same data yields different dendrograms per rule.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Linkage visibly changes merge trees on the same data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Features are inputs; linkage reads distances.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Linkage consumes the metric; it does not replace it.

medium.prompt: How do you get flat clusters from hierarchical clustering?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.body: Always cut at the root into one cluster.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Always cut into n singleton clusters.

medium.hint: Next step: draw a horizontal line across the merge tree.
medium.explanation: Dendrogram cuts choose granularity; height sets cluster count and scale.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: merges stack from leaves to root with heights. Step 2: a horizontal cut at height h yields the clusters below it. Step 3: higher cuts give fewer, coarser groups. Step 4: no automatic truth; root and leaves are trivial extremes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The tree nests all scales; you choose the cut.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Root cut gives one blob: valid but trivial.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Leaf cut memorizes every point: trivial.

medium.prompt: Two blobs join via a thin noise trail. Which linkage merges them wrongly?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Single linkage chains through noise bridges; complete linkage resists them.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Complete linkage chains worst; single resists bridges.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Linkage never affects noise sensitivity.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Noise bridges help every linkage equally.

medium.hint: Next step: ask what single close pair can trigger.
medium.explanation: Min-distance merging chains across bridges; max-distance demands full cohesion.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: a thin noise trail links two blobs. Step 2: single needs one close pair to merge, so it leaks across. Step 3: complete needs all pairs close, so the bridge fails the test. Step 4: swapping the roles reverses the documented behavior.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Reversed: complete is the bridge-resistant rule.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Chaining sensitivity is linkage's famous difference.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Bridges corrupt single-link merges specifically.

medium.prompt: Misses cost 10× false alarms. How do you pick the operating threshold from the ROC curve?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Always use threshold 0.5 no matter the error costs.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Pick the single point with maximum AUC.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Slide to a high-TPR point minimizing cost-weighted errors (e.g. 10·FN + FP).

choices.label: D
choices.body: Always maximize accuracy along the curve.

medium.hint: Next step: weight each error type by its cost along the curve.
medium.explanation: ROC lists every tradeoff; error costs pick the operating point, favoring recall here.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: each ROC point is one threshold's (FPR, TPR). Step 2: misses cost 10× alarms, so total cost = 10·FN + FP. Step 3: slide up the curve to the minimum-cost point in the high-TPR region. Step 4: fixed 0.5 or max-accuracy ignore the skew; AUC summarizes the curve, it is not a point.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 0.5 assumes equal costs; skewed costs shift the optimum.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: AUC summarizes the whole curve; it is not a selectable point.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Accuracy weights errors equally, contradicting the 10× skew.

hard.prompt: Your classifier reaches 0% train error. Does that prove it is a good model?

choices.label: A

hard.deepDive: Step 1: memorize all 1000 train rows exactly. Step 2: train error is 0%. Step 3: on 500 new rows the table has no entry and guesses, scoring ~50%. Step 4: optimization success and pattern learning are different achievements.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Memorization also gives 0 train error without learning any pattern.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Optimization minimizes train loss; generalization needs held-out proof.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Rich models hit 0 train error routinely; impossibility is false.

hard.prompt: Which score pair shows memorization on balanced binary labels?

hard.explanation: Perfect train with chance-level test is the fingerprint of memorization.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: gap = 100 - 52 = 48 points. Step 2: test near chance on balanced classes means no pattern captured. Step 3: matched 100/99 would be genuine learning. Step 4: matched low scores are underfitting, not overfitting.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Matched near-perfect scores mean real generalization.

hard.prompt: With 20% random label noise, a deep tree still hits 100% train accuracy. Why?

choices.label: A

choices.body: Label noise makes 100% train accuracy impossible.

choices.body: Label noise only affects the test set, never training.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Label noise is fixed by training longer.

hard.explanation: Noisy labels are memorizable, inflating train while depressing test.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: flip 20% of train labels at random. Step 2: a deep tree memorizes even the flipped rows, reaching ~100% train. Step 3: on clean test rows those memorized flips hurt, lowering test. Step 4: longer training worsens this memorization rather than fixing it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Rich models can fit even random labels given capacity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Noise in train directly shapes the fitted model.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: More epochs deepen memorization of noise; restraint helps instead.

hard.prompt: A vision model tuned on day images fails on night images. What broke?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Test accuracy collapses because the test distribution differs (train iid broken).

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.body: Test accuracy collapses because the test set is too large.

choices.label: D

hard.explanation: Generalization assumes same distribution; shift breaks the test estimate's meaning.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: train on daytime road images only. Step 2: test on night images. Step 3: the iid assumption, same distribution for train and test, fails. Step 4: train scores stay high while night-test scores fall, a shift problem not an underfit.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Underfit would show low train scores too; here train is high.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Larger test only sharpens the estimate; it cannot collapse accuracy.

hard.prompt: Which evaluation suffers distribution shift?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A flu model trained in 2019 tested during a 2020 outbreak regime.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A flu model trained and tested on random splits of 2019 visits.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A flu model with more 2019 training rows.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A flu model evaluated with cross-validation inside 2019.

hard.hint: Next step: ask whether train and deployment draws come from one distribution.
hard.explanation: Temporal shift makes old-test scores stale for the new regime.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: random 2019 splits share one regime. Step 2: 2020 brings new prevalence and behavior. Step 3: P(y|x) or P(x) changed, so 2019-test optimism misleads. Step 4: more 2019 rows or 2019-only CV cannot reveal the new regime.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Same-year random splits satisfy iid; no shift is involved.

hard.prompt: Live loan applicants differ from 2022 training rows. What is the principled fix?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Collect deployment-like data or reweight; the iid assumption failed.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Tune harder on the old test set until scores recover.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Shrink the test set to hide the drop.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Report train accuracy instead of test.

hard.hint: Next step: change the data to match deployment, not the meter.
hard.explanation: Fix shift with matching data, not with test-set hill-climbing.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: diagnose shift between train and live inputs. Step 2: sample fresh live-like rows for validation. Step 3: reweight or retrain toward the live mix. Step 4: tuning on stale test or hiding test fakes the number without fixing mismatch.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Hill-climbing stale test overfits the old regime.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Smaller test only noisifies the bad estimate.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Train accuracy ignores the deployment mismatch entirely.

hard.prompt: Model A beats B by 5 points on a 20-sample test (80% vs 75%). Is that conclusive?

choices.label: A
choices.body: About ±10 points: a 20-sample test is too noisy for 5-point claims.

choices.label: B
choices.body: About ±0.1 points: 20 samples pin accuracy precisely.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Exactly 0: any test set gives the exact true accuracy.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Noise depends only on model size, not test size.

hard.hint: Next step: estimate sqrt(p(1-p)/n) for the test size.
hard.explanation: Tiny test sets have large standard errors; small gaps are inconclusive.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: each test row is a Bernoulli trial near p=0.8. Step 2: standard error ≈ sqrt(0.8·0.2/20) ≈ 9 points. Step 3: a 5-point gap between models is inside that noise. Step 4: claiming a winner from ±10-point noise overstates evidence.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 20 samples give ~9-point noise, not sub-point precision.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Test accuracy estimates truth with sampling error; exactness is false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Estimate variance shrinks with test size n, not model size.

hard.prompt: Model X leads by 2 points on n=50; model Y leads by 2 points on n=5000. Who is more trustworthy?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: Model Y on 5000 samples; big test sets are less trustworthy.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Both equally; test size never matters.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Neither; accuracy needs no uncertainty.

hard.hint: Next step: compare 1/sqrt(n) for the two test sizes.
hard.explanation: Bigger test sets shrink the error bars; small-test leads may be noise.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: standard error scales as 1/sqrt(n). Step 2: n=50 gives ~7-point noise near 90%. Step 3: n=5000 gives ~0.7-point noise. Step 4: a 2-point lead on n=50 is inside noise while on n=5000 it is solid.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Large test sets tighten intervals; they are more trustworthy.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Test size directly sets interval width via 1/sqrt(n).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Every estimate needs error bars before claiming a winner.

hard.prompt: After 30 tweaks guided by a 100-sample test, what should you do before claiming victory?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Widen test with fresh rows; tuning on the same 100 overfits it.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.body: Report the best of 30 peeks as the final accuracy.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Shrink test to the 10 easiest rows.

hard.explanation: Reused small tests overfit; refresh the test or hold out a new one.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: 30 rounds of test-guided tweaks select luck on those 100 rows. Step 2: the 100-sample meter itself degrades with reuse. Step 3: fresh rows restore an unbiased read. Step 4: reporting the max of 30 peeks or cherry-picking rows bakes in optimism.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: More hill-climbing on the same rows deepens test overfitting.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Best-of-30 is a selection-biased maximum, not an estimate.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Easy-row cherry-picking inflates the score artificially.

hard.prompt: Raising the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.9 does what to precision and recall?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: Threshold 0.9: more positives and higher recall.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Threshold has no effect on predictions.

choices.label: D

hard.explanation: Higher thresholds trade recall for precision.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Higher bars fire less often, so recall falls, not rises.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Threshold directly flips labels near the boundary.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Accuracy depends on data mix, not on the threshold number.

hard.prompt: Missing fraud costs 100× a false alarm. How should you move the threshold?

hard.deepDive: Step 1: missing fraud costs far more than a false alarm. Step 2: lowering the bar flags more transactions. Step 3: recall rises since fewer frauds slip through. Step 4: precision dips, the accepted price; raising the bar would do the opposite.

wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Threshold acts after training on the decision rule.

hard.prompt: Why is logistic regression optimization considered easy and reliable?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Logistic loss is convex: one global minimum, no spurious valleys.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.body: Logistic loss has no minimum at all.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Infeasible QP has no solution when overlap exists.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Deleting the hard rows biases the problem definition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Overlap changes feasibility; method must adapt.

hard.prompt: Why accept training violations in a soft-margin SVM?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Soft-margin tolerates training crossings to protect new-data accuracy.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Soft-margin guarantees zero training errors.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Soft-margin forbids all violations strictly.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Soft-margin ignores the margin entirely.

hard.hint: Next step: read the slack term as paid permission to cross.
hard.explanation: Slack buys crossings at price C to keep streets smooth and general.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: slack ξᵢ ≥ 0 permits y·f ≥ 1 − ξᵢ. Step 2: Σξᵢ priced by C. Step 3: some train rows cross for a smoother street. Step 4: zero-error and forbid-all describe hard margins, not soft.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Zero train error is the hard-margin demand that overlap forbids.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Forbidding is hard-margin; soft explicitly permits.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Margin stays central; slack only softens its enforcement.

hard.prompt: Where does feature scaling belong in a kernel SVM pipeline?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Scale-then-kernel: standardize first or distances (hence K) distort.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Kernel-then-scale: scale the Gram matrix rows arbitrarily.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Skip scaling; kernels self-normalize.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Scale only the labels, never features.

hard.hint: Next step: trace where raw scales enter K.
hard.explanation: Standardize features before kernel computation, using train-only stats.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: RBF/polynomial use dot products and distances. Step 2: raw income-vs-age scales skew those inputs. Step 3: standardizing features first balances K. Step 4: post-hoc Gram scaling and label-only scaling miss the input distortion.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Gram fiddling cannot undo input-scale domination.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Kernels amplify scale effects; they do not cancel them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Labels set the task; feature scales drive K.

hard.prompt: What is the leak-free protocol for tuning a kernel SVM?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Fit scaler on train, apply to val/test; tune C and γ on validation.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Fit scaler on all data including test, then tune on test.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Skip validation; report train accuracy with kernels.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Tune γ on test for the final report.

hard.hint: Next step: check which rows each fitting step sees.
hard.explanation: Leak-free kernel tuning: train-only scaling, validation grid, one test read.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: scaler stats from train only keep test quarantined. Step 2: grid over (C, γ) scored on validation. Step 3: freeze the winner, score once on test. Step 4: pooled scaling or test tuning leaks the judge.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Pooled stats and test tuning both leak test into choices.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Train accuracy with kernels memorizes; it proves nothing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: γ tuned on test biases the final report upward.

hard.prompt: In the SVM dual, what does sparsity of α mean?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Most αᵢ are 0; predictions sum only over support vectors.

choices.label: B
choices.body: All αᵢ are nonzero and equal.

choices.label: C
choices.body: αᵢ values are the test labels.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Dual variables have no link to support vectors.

hard.hint: Next step: ask which αᵢ survive complementary slackness.
hard.explanation: Dual sparsity is support-vector sparsity: only αᵢ > 0 rows predict.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: dual maximizes over αᵢ ≥ 0 with Σ αᵢyᵢ = 0. Step 2: KKT complementarity zeroes αᵢ for strictly-satisfied rows. Step 3: survivors (αᵢ > 0) are the supports. Step 4: f(x) = Σ αᵢyᵢK(xᵢ,x) + b sums survivors only.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Uniform nonzero α would mean every row binds, atypical.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: α are train weights, never test labels.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: α > 0 is literally the support-vector indicator.

hard.prompt: One mislabeled outlier drags your SVM street sideways. What C fix?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Small C tolerates the outlier (pays small slack) to keep a smooth street.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Huge C must always be used despite the outlier.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Delete the test set to accommodate the outlier.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Outliers prove SVMs cannot be used at all.

hard.hint: Next step: price the slack for satisfying versus ignoring the outlier.
hard.explanation: Small C lets the street eat outlier slack instead of pivoting to it.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: one flipped label sits deep in opposite territory. Step 2: huge C pivots the whole street to satisfy it. Step 3: small C pays ξ > 1 cheaply and holds the street. Step 4: validation confirms the smoother street scores higher on fresh rows.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Huge C obeys the outlier hardest; the pivot worsens.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Test data is irrelevant to fitting the street.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Soft margins exist precisely to survive outliers.

hard.prompt: How is the SVM bias term b recovered from the dual solution?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Margin supports (0 < α < C) fix b via y·f = 1; bounded ones (α = C) sit inside.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The bias b is always zero in SVMs.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Bounded support vectors lie exactly on the margin.

choices.label: D
choices.body: b is tuned on the test set.

hard.hint: Next step: separate supports that sit on the street edge from capped ones.
hard.explanation: Unbounded margin supports pin the bias; C-capped rows are slack cases.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: KKT splits supports: margin vs bounded. Step 2: margin supports satisfy y·f = 1 exactly, pinning b = y − Σ αyK. Step 3: bounded (α = C) tolerate y·f < 1, inside or across. Step 4: b is solved from train margin rows, never zero-forced or test-tuned.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: b shifts the street; zeroing it is an extra (usually wrong) constraint.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Reversed: capped rows leave the edge; free ones hold it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: b comes from train margin rows, never test.

hard.prompt: A fraud model reports 99% accuracy on 1% fraud data. Why might that be worthless?

choices.label: A
choices.body: 99% accuracy with 0% recall: the metric hides total minority failure.

choices.label: B
choices.body: 99% accuracy proves the fraud detector is excellent.

choices.label: C
choices.body: 99% accuracy means 99% of frauds were caught.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Imbalance makes accuracy more reliable, not less.

hard.hint: Next step: score the do-nothing classifier first.
hard.explanation: Accuracy on 99-to-1 data rewards the lazy all-negative classifier.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: 1000 rows, 10 frauds, all-negative verdicts. Step 2: accuracy = 990/1000 = 99%. Step 3: recall = 0/10 = 0%, precision undefined-to-0. Step 4: the headline number celebrates catching nothing.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Zero frauds caught contradicts excellence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 99% counts mostly negatives; fraud recall is 0%.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Reversed: imbalance is exactly when accuracy collapses as a guide.

hard.prompt: How should you evaluate classifiers on 1%-positive data?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Report precision/recall/F1 or PR-AUC on the minority alongside rates.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Report accuracy alone; it suffices.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Report training accuracy instead of test metrics.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Report only the majority-class accuracy.

hard.hint: Next step: ask which metric notices the 10 frauds at all.
hard.explanation: Minority-aware metrics plus the confusion details replace headline accuracy.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: accuracy saturates near 99% for any lazy model. Step 2: PR-AUC focuses on positive ranking across thresholds. Step 3: F1 pins one operating point's balance. Step 4: train and majority-only numbers hide deployment failure equally.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Accuracy is swamped by negatives; it cannot see frauds.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Train numbers add optimism on top of blindness.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Majority-only scoring ignores the class of interest.

hard.prompt: Why can ROC-AUC flatter a fraud model that PR-AUC condemns?

choices.label: A
choices.body: ROC-AUC can look rosy (few FPs among many negatives) while PR-AUC exposes poor precision.

choices.label: B
choices.body: ROC-AUC and PR-AUC always agree on imbalanced data.

choices.label: C
choices.body: PR-AUC is always higher than ROC-AUC.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Neither curve applies to imbalanced tasks.

hard.hint: Next step: dilute 50 false alarms across 990 negatives vs 10 positives.
hard.explanation: Big negative pools dilute FPR; precision-focused views stay honest.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: 10 frauds, 990 legit; 50 false alarms give FPR ≈ 5%, TPR 80%. Step 2: ROC point (0.05, 0.8) looks strong. Step 3: precision = 8/58 ≈ 14%: poor. Step 4: PR-AUC punishes the alarm flood that ROC dilutes across negatives.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: They diverge exactly when negatives dominate.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No fixed ordering holds; PR-AUC is usually lower here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Both apply; PR-AUC is the stricter lens for rare positives.

hard.prompt: How does k-means++ initialization improve on uniform random starts?

choices.label: A
choices.body: K-means++ spreads starts (distant points likelier), cutting bad local minima.

choices.label: B
choices.body: K-means++ stacks all centroids at the data mean.

choices.label: C
choices.body: K-means++ uses true labels for seeding.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Seeding never affects the final clusters.

hard.hint: Next step: ask which points should seed next given current picks.
hard.explanation: Distance-weighted seeding starts centroids in different regions for better optima.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: pick first centroid uniformly. Step 2: weight each point by squared distance to chosen set. Step 3: distant regions seed next with high probability. Step 4: spread starts land near distinct blobs; stacking and labels contradict the method.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Stacking wastes centroids; spreading is the point.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Labels are unavailable; distances drive the weighting.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Seeding decides which local minimum you land in.

hard.prompt: K-means fails on two interleaved crescents. Why won't more restarts fix it?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Elongated/stretched blobs split wrongly: one true cluster, two k-means halves.

choices.label: B
choices.body: K-means handles any cluster shape perfectly.

choices.label: C
choices.body: K-means only fails on spherical blobs.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Shape sensitivity is fixed by adding more random restarts.

hard.hint: Next step: draw the straight borders k-means must produce.
hard.explanation: Spherical Voronoi bias breaks on non-convex shapes; restarts cannot fix bias.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: two crescent moons interlock. Step 2: k-means draws straight Voronoi borders. Step 3: crescents get sliced across their curves. Step 4: restarts resample the same spherical bias; shape mismatch persists.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Spherical bias is k-means' documented shape limit.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Reversed: spheres are its best case, crescents the failure.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Restarts fight local minima, not model bias.

hard.prompt: A k-means centroid ends up with no assigned points. What should you do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Empty clusters can strand: reinitialize or drop them and continue.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Empty clusters are impossible in k-means.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Stop the whole run and report failure.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Fill empty centroids with test points.

hard.hint: Next step: compute the mean of zero assigned points.
hard.explanation: Dead centroids need reseeding or removal; the run otherwise continues.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: a centroid loses all members after reassignment. Step 2: its mean is undefined. Step 3: common fixes: reseed at a far point or drop to k−1. Step 4: impossibility is false, full stops wasteful, test-filling leaks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Poor starts strand centroids routinely.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Reseeding salvages the run; quitting wastes it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Test rows must never enter training state.

hard.prompt: Income (thousands) and age (years) feed k-means. What preprocessing and why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Standardize, or income-axis gaps swallow age-axis structure.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Raw scales are fine; distances self-balance.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Multiply income by 1000× to help clustering.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Scaling only matters for supervised models.

hard.hint: Next step: compare squared ranges axis by axis.
hard.explanation: Distance clustering is scale-ruled; standardize so axes vote fairly.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: income gaps ~10⁴, age gaps ~10¹. Step 2: squared Euclidean sums are ~10⁸ vs ~10² per axis. Step 3: age contributes ~0.0001% of distances: invisible. Step 4: unit-variance scaling restores each axis's vote; stretching worsens it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Raw ranges let one axis dictate every distance.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Stretching deepens the domination further.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Distance methods are the most scale-sensitive of all.

hard.prompt: How should k-means handle a zip-code feature?

choices.label: A
choices.body: One-hot + Hamming/Jaccard or k-modes; means of zip codes are nonsense.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Encode zip codes as integers and take Euclidean means.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Drop all categorical features always.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Distances work on raw strings directly.

hard.hint: Next step: interpret the mean of two zip codes.
hard.explanation: Nominal features need matching-based distances, not numeric means.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: zip 90210 vs 10001: numeric gap is meaningless. Step 2: their mean 50105.5 is a zip nowhere. Step 3: one-hot with matching distances respects category identity. Step 4: dropping everything wastes signal; raw strings have no metric.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Integer gaps and means of codes are arbitrary fictions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: blanket deletion discards real segment signal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Strings need encoded distances first.

hard.prompt: K-means degrades on 1000-dimensional data with 20 real signals. Why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Curse of dimensionality: distances concentrate, neighbors lose contrast.

choices.label: B
choices.body: More dimensions always sharpen distance contrast.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Dimensionality never affects distances.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The fix is always more clusters, never fewer features.

hard.hint: Next step: compare nearest and farthest distances in high dims.
hard.explanation: High-dimensional distances concentrate; reduce dimensions before clustering.
hard.deepDive: Step 1: in 1000 noisy dims, pairwise distances crowd near one value. Step 2: nearest vs farthest differ by ~1%. Step 3: assignment becomes near-arbitrary. Step 4: PCA/feature selection restores contrast; more clusters cannot.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Reversed: contrast fades as dims grow.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Concentration is the documented high-dim effect.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Fewer, better features beat more clusters here.
